chapter_title: Initial Device Configuration and Management Access
chapter_summary:
Getting a new Juniper device up and running for the first time is an exciting step! Your journey begins with establishing initial management access. For any brand-new device, or one that has been factory reset, the primary method of access is typically through the **console port**. This is an out-of-band management interface, meaning it doesn't rely on the network itself being operational. You'll need a console cable (often an RJ-45 to DB-9 serial cable) and a terminal emulator program (like PuTTY, SecureCRT, or minicom) on your computer. Connect the console cable from your computer's serial port (or a USB-to-serial adapter) to the console port on the Juniper device. Configure your terminal emulator with the standard serial settings: 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, no flow control. Once connected, power on the device, and you'll see the boot sequence and eventually land at the Junos OS CLI operational prompt (`>`).

The very first and most critical configuration step is to set the **root password**. Without it, anyone with console access can gain full control of your device. From the operational mode prompt (`>`), you'll enter configuration mode by typing `configure` or `edit`. The prompt will change to `#`. From here, the command to set the root password is `set system root-authentication plain-text-password`. You'll be prompted to enter and confirm the password. While `plain-text-password` is used for initial setup, it's a common mistake to leave it as plain text. For production environments, consider using `encrypted-password` or integrating with external authentication systems like RADIUS or TACACS+. After setting the password, you must `commit` the changes for them to become active. The `commit` command saves the configuration to the device's persistent storage and activates it. If you make a mistake before committing, you can use `rollback 0` to revert to the last committed configuration.

Once the root password is set, the next crucial step is to configure **out-of-band (OOB) management access**. This allows you to manage the device remotely over the network, rather than requiring a physical console connection. Juniper devices typically use the `me0` (management Ethernet) or `fxp0` interface for this purpose. This interface is physically separate from the data plane interfaces and is dedicated solely to management traffic. You'll configure an IP address and subnet mask on this interface, and optionally a default gateway if your management network is not directly connected.

Here's an example of configuring the `me0` interface:
```
edit
set interfaces me0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.1.10/24
set system services ssh
set system services telnet # (Use SSH for production, Telnet for initial setup only)
set system services web-management http # (Optional, for J-Web GUI)
set system services web-management https # (Optional, for secure J-Web GUI)
set system host-name JNCIS-Router-1
set system domain-name cohortia.local
set system name-server 8.8.8.8
set system ntp server 0.pool.ntp.org
set system time-zone America/New_York
set system syslog user * any info
set system syslog file messages any notice
set system syslog file interactive-commands interactive-commands any
commit and-quit
```
In this example, we've configured an IP address, enabled SSH for secure remote CLI access (always prefer SSH over Telnet for security!), set a hostname and domain name, configured DNS, NTP, and basic syslog. The `commit and-quit` command saves the configuration and exits configuration mode.

Beyond the root user, it's best practice to create **additional local user accounts** with specific privileges. This adheres to the principle of least privilege, where users only have the access they need. You can define user accounts and assign them to various Junos OS login classes, which determine their permissions. For instance, the `super-user` class grants full administrative access, while `read-only` provides monitoring capabilities without configuration rights.

Example of creating a new user:
```
edit
set system login user student uid 2000 class super-user authentication plain-text-password
# (Enter password when prompted)
commit and-quit
```
**Safety Note:** Always ensure that your management interfaces are protected by firewalls or access control lists (ACLs) to restrict access to trusted sources only. Disabling unused management services (like Telnet or HTTP if not needed) is also a critical security measure. Regularly review your management access configurations and user accounts. A common mistake is leaving default credentials or easily guessable passwords, which are prime targets for attackers. Always use strong, unique passwords and consider multi-factor authentication where possible.

Finally, remember the power of the `rollback` command. If you make a configuration change that causes an issue, you can quickly revert to a previous working configuration. `rollback 0` reverts to the last committed configuration. You can also `rollback <number>` to revert to a specific previous configuration (Junos OS stores the last 50 committed configurations by default). This transactional approach significantly reduces the risk associated with making changes on a live device.

screens.title: Initial Device Configuration and Management Access
screens.subtitle: Establish secure, reliable management access to a fresh Juniper device

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you'll learn the first essential steps for bringing a Juniper device into service. We start by establishing a console connection so you can reach the Junos OS on a factory-default device. Then you will set a strong root password, configure a dedicated out-of-band management interface such as me0 or fxp0, and enable secure remote access methods like SSH. Along the way we cover other best-practice items you should configure early: a hostname and domain, name servers, NTP, basic syslog, and creating least-privilege local accounts. You will also learn the Junos transactional model — commit and rollback — which protects live equipment from accidental changes. Each item matters: console access gives you recovery options when the network is down; the management interface keeps administration traffic off the data plane; SSH and careful account management reduce attack surface; and rollback lets you recover quickly from mistakes. By the end of these screens you'll be able to perform the hands-on initial setup steps and verify the device is reachable and secure. Think about the first command you would type on a fresh box and why that password choice matters.

keyIdea.text: Console for access, set root password, configure me0/fxp0 for OOB, enable SSH, use commit and rollback, and create least-privilege users.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These four objectives frame the practical skills you'll take away. First, you will be able to connect to a new Juniper device using the console port and the correct serial parameters. That means understanding why the console is out-of-band and how it helps when the network is unavailable. Second, you'll perform initial setup steps including setting a strong root password and committing configuration safely; this prevents unauthorized access and preserves operational state. Third, you'll configure out-of-band management on me0 or fxp0, assign an IP, and set a gateway and DNS, so the device is reachable by administrators without touching the data plane. Fourth, you will create and manage local user accounts and assign login classes so users have least privilege. Each objective includes a short practice skill — connecting, entering configuration mode, using set commands, committing or rolling back changes, and verifying with show commands. As you progress, compare secure versus insecure defaults and practice the habit of enabling SSH and disabling Telnet or HTTP unless strictly required. These objectives combine command skill with a security mindset you will use every time you bring up a device.

keyIdea.text: Console access, root password, OOB management, user accounts and secure services with commit/rollback confidence.

narration.text: In this second objectives slide we'll break the skills into command-level practices so you know precisely what to try in a lab. First, enter configuration mode from the operational prompt by typing configure or edit — this moves you into candidate configuration where set commands apply. Second, practice the set commands used for initial setup: set system root-authentication plain-text-password, set interfaces me0 unit 0 family inet address, set system services ssh, and set system host-name. Fourth, verify your work with show system host-name and show interfaces me0 terse. Each skill links a command to a purpose: passwords secure access, me0 creates reachability, services enable remote management, and verification confirms success. Practicing these ensures you can bring a device online safely and confidently in real deployments.

screens.title: Console Port and Out-of-Band Access
screens.subtitle: Why the console is the first contact and how OOB management differs from the data plane

narration.text: A new or factory-reset Juniper device is most reliably reached through the console port. The console is a physical serial interface that provides direct, out-of-band access to the device's operating system; it does not depend on any network configuration or services. To use it you need a console cable and a terminal emulator configured with standard serial settings: 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, and no flow control. When you power on the device with a console attached, you will see boot messages and eventually reach the Junos operational prompt. Out-of-band management uses a dedicated Ethernet interface such as me0 or fxp0 that is logically and often physically separate from the data plane. Unlike the console, me0 carries IP traffic so you can manage the device remotely over a management network. The distinction matters: the console is your recovery and initial setup path. me0 or fxp0 is your long-term management path and should be placed on a secured management VLAN or network. A common misconception is treating a data-plane interface as management — that exposes management traffic to normal routing and increases risk. Example: if the production network is down, only the console or a separately routed OOB network can restore access. Key takeaway: always verify console connectivity first, then configure a secure OOB IP on me0 or fxp0 so routine administration does not require physical access.

keyIdea.title: Console vs OOB
keyIdea.text: Console is physical and always available at first boot; me0/fxp0 provides remote management over a dedicated management network.

content.html:
Core Concept › Console & OOB
Console Port and Out-of-Band Access
Direct serial access for initial setup, and dedicated management Ethernet for remote administration.
Definition and setup
Console: RJ-45/DB-9 or USB-to-serial cable, terminal emulator standard settings. OOB: me0 or fxp0 assigned an IP and gateway on a management network.
Serial settings: 9600 baud 8 data bits no parity 1 stop bit no flow control
Common misconception
Treating a data-plane interface as management may leave the device unreachable when the data network fails.
Key takeaway
Console is recovery-first; me0/fxp0 is the recommended long-term management path when secured properly.
Example scenario
You power a factory-default router. Using a USB-to-serial adapter and a terminal, you observe the boot messages and press Enter to reach the prompt. You use this session to set the root password and configure me0 with an IP so you can later SSH from a management workstation.
Explanation bullets
  • Console access bypasses network dependencies during initial bring-up.
  • me0/fxp0 isolates management traffic from production routing and switching.
  • Place management interfaces on a protected management VLAN and control access via ACLs or firewalls.

screens.title: Console Connection and Terminal Settings
screens.subtitle: Physical cable, terminal configuration, and what to expect during boot

narration.text: Connecting to a Juniper device via the console is a short, repeatable process that removes network dependency for initial access. First, choose the correct cable type — many devices use an RJ-45 to DB-9 serial cable or a USB-to-serial adapter if your laptop lacks a serial port. Second, open a terminal emulator and configure the serial session: 9600 baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, and no flow control. This exact setting prevents garbled output on most Juniper hardware. Third, power on the device with the console attached and observe the boot text. You should see kernel messages and Junos initialization lines until you reach the operational prompt marked by a greater-than symbol. Fourth, if the console appears blank, check cable seating, COM port selection, and adapter drivers on your host. A common misconception is that higher baud rates improve responsiveness; for initial configuration, stick with the device recommended 9600 to avoid missed characters. Example: you connect a USB adapter, open a session at 9600, and after power-up you press Enter and receive the > prompt. This gives you the operational shell to run configure and begin setup. Practice this sequence so you can recover hardware without network access.

keyIdea.title: Quick process
keyIdea.text: Cable, terminal settings, boot observation, verify prompt; troubleshoot blank console by checking cabling and host settings.

content.html:
Process Flow › Console Connection
Step-by-step
1. Cable
Use RJ-45 to DB-9 or a USB-to-serial adapter and ensure solid connections.
2. Terminal settings
Set 9600/8/N/1, no flow control in your emulator.
3. Power & observe
Power the device, watch boot messages, and wait for the operational prompt.
Troubleshoot
Blank screen? Check COM port, cable seating, and adapter drivers on your host OS.
Example session
Power on device, then in terminal emulator you see: Junos OS ... loading ... login: >
When you reach the > prompt, you can run show or type configure to enter # configuration mode. This is the point to set the root password and perform initial configuration steps.
Key takeaway
Console setup is deterministic. Practice the flow until confident in troubleshooting adapter issues.

screens.title: Root Password and Configuration Mode
screens.subtitle: How to protect the root account and use Junos configuration mode safely

narration.text: The root user on a Junos device has full administrative authority. Setting a strong root password immediately after initial access is critical to prevent unauthorized control. To change this password you first need to enter configuration mode from the operational prompt by typing configure or edit; the prompt changes to indicate configuration mode. Then issue the set system root-authentication plain-text-password command and follow the password prompts. While plain-text-password is convenient during initial setup, do not leave insecure defaults in production. Where available, use encrypted-password or integrate external authentication such as RADIUS or TACACS+ for better control. After making changes, remember to run commit to save and apply them. The Junos commit is transactional: if you make a mistake you can use rollback 0 to return to the last committed state. A common mistake is to set a password but forget to commit, leaving the device with an unchanged root password. Example: you type configure, set the root password, then commit and-quit to apply and exit configuration mode. Always verify by attempting an authenticated session or checking the configuration after commit. Takeaway: set strong passwords, commit changes, and use rollback to recover from errors rather than guessing reversal commands.

keyIdea.title: Protect root
keyIdea.text: Enter configure, set root-authentication, commit changes, and use rollback to recover if needed.

content.html:
Definition › Root Password & Config Mode
What to do
From the > prompt enter configuration mode, set the root password, and commit to apply.
configure
set system root-authentication plain-text-password
# enter and confirm password prompts
commit and-quit
Common mistake
Forgetting to commit leaves the old password active and creates a false sense of security.
Why this matters
The root account controls everything. A weak or default root password is the easiest path for an attacker to gain full control of the device.
Pro tip
Prefer encrypted-password or central auth for long-term security; use plain-text only for initial lab setup when necessary.
Check
After commit, verify by attempting an authenticated session or viewing committed configuration entries.

screens.title: Configure the me0 Interface and Basic Services
screens.subtitle: Assign an IP to me0, enable SSH, and set hostname, DNS, and NTP

narration.text: Configuring me0 provides out-of-band IP reachability for management. Use configuration mode to add an address to the interface, enable SSH for secure remote CLI access, and set host and system services you depend on. The canonical sequence is to edit, set interfaces me0 unit 0 family inet address with an appropriate IP and mask, set system services ssh, set system host-name, and then commit. Also set DNS and NTP to ensure the device can resolve names and keep accurate time, which is important for certificate validation and log timestamps. Below is a code walkthrough you can type or paste in a lab. After commit and-quit you should verify the interface and services with show commands. A common misconception is that enabling HTTP is safe by default; prefer HTTPS for any web management and disable unused services. Example: set interfaces me0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.100.1/24, set system services ssh, set system name-server 8.8.8.8, set system ntp server 0. pool. ntp. org, and then commit. Always verify with show interfaces me0 terse and show system services to confirm reachability and that SSH is listening. This ensures your OOB management is functional and auditable.

keyIdea.title: me0 + services
keyIdea.text: Set me0 address, enable SSH, configure hostname, DNS and NTP, then commit and verify with show commands.

Code Walkthrough › me0 & Services
Configure the me0 Interface and Basic Services
Add an IP to me0, enable SSH, and set host and system services before committing.
Configuration template

set interfaces me0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.100.1/24
set system services ssh
set system host-name JNCIS-Core-R1
set system domain-name cohortia.local
set system name-server 8.8.8.8
set system ntp server 0.pool.ntp.org
set system time-zone America/New_York
commit and-quit
Verify

Security note
Prefer SSH over Telnet; if you enable web-management use HTTPS only and restrict access with ACLs.

screens.title: Management Services: SSH vs Telnet vs Web
screens.subtitle: Choose secure services and disable unused ones

narration.text: Management services control how administrators connect to the device. SSH provides an encrypted command-line session and is the recommended production option. Telnet sends credentials and session data in clear text and should be used only in controlled, initial lab setups if necessary. Web-management can be convenient, but plain HTTP is insecure; prefer HTTPS when enabling web access. The chapter lists commands to enable each service: set system services ssh, set system services telnet, set system services web-management http or https. A common misconception is that enabling both SSH and Telnet adds redundancy; in reality Telnet increases attack surface and rarely adds useful redundancy if SSH is available. Instead, focus on securing SSH with strong host keys and limiting which management hosts can reach me0 with ACLs or firewall rules. Example: enable SSH only, add an ACL on your management switch or firewall to permit just known administrator IPs, and avoid enabling HTTP or Telnet unless required. Key takeaway: enable the minimally necessary, secure service set and pair services with network-level restrictions to protect the management plane. Management Services: SSH vs Telnet vs Web means use ssh for remote management, avoid telnet and http in production, and protect services with acls.. In practical terms, choose secure services and disable unused ones. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Service selection
keyIdea.text: Use SSH for remote management, avoid Telnet and HTTP in production, and protect services with ACLs.

content.html:
Comparison › SSH vs Telnet vs Web
SSH
Encrypted CLI access suitable for production. Use set system services ssh and protect with ACLs.
Best practice: enable only SSH and restrict source addresses.
Telnet
Unencrypted and insecure. Use only for constrained lab scenarios. Prefer disabling in production.
Avoid in production
Web-management
HTTP is insecure; HTTPS is acceptable when necessary. Consider J-Web HTTPS with strict access controls.
Tip: disable HTTP, enable only HTTPS if needed
Example
set system services ssh and restrict access via ACLs on the management network to known admin IPs.
Misconception
Enabling more services does not make a device safer; it increases attack surface.

screens.title: Hostname, DNS, NTP, Time Zone, and Syslog
screens.subtitle: Configure system identity and time services for reliable operations and logs

narration.text: A device's hostname and system-level services are small but critical pieces of configuration. Set a clear, descriptive hostname so logs, alerts, and management interfaces identify the device confidently. Configure a domain name and name-server so the device can resolve hostnames, and set NTP servers and time zone so logs and certificates have accurate timestamps. Syslog configuration controls where system messages are stored and which events are logged; this is essential for troubleshooting and audit trails. In practice, you will add commands such as set system host-name, set system domain-name, set system name-server, and set system ntp server. Also configure basic syslog files and interactive-commands logs as needed. A common oversight is neglecting NTP, which leads to inconsistent timestamps between devices and complicates event correlation. Example: set system host-name JNCIS-Router-1, set system name-server 8.8.8.8, set system ntp server 0. pool. ntp. org, then commit. After committing, check system time and syslog status. Key takeaway: these small settings make monitoring, authentication, and auditing work reliably across your network. Hostname, DNS, NTP, Time Zone, and Syslog means hostname, dns, ntp, time zone, and syslog must be configured early for consistent logs, certificates, and monitoring.. In practical terms, configure system identity and time services for reliable operations and logs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: System services
keyIdea.text: Hostname, DNS, NTP, time zone, and syslog must be configured early for consistent logs, certificates, and monitoring.

Check

screens.title: Local User Accounts and Login Classes
screens.subtitle: Create users and assign permissions following least privilege

narration.text: Beyond the root account, create local user accounts with carefully scoped permissions. Junos uses login classes to define what a user can do; common classes include super-user for full administrative rights and read-only for monitoring-only access. The recommended approach is to assign users the minimal privileges they need to perform their job. To create a user, enter configuration mode and use set system login user uid class authentication plain-text-password. After you set a password and commit, that account exists on the device. A concrete example is creating a student account with super-user or a limited class depending on the lab: set system login user student uid 2000 class super-user authentication plain-text-password. Be aware that plain-text-password is convenient for labs but consider encrypted-password or central authentication for production. A misconception is that many administrators should share the root account; instead, create individual accounts for auditing and accountability. Key takeaway: use individual accounts with login classes, apply least privilege, and review accounts regularly to remove unused entries or change passwords periodically. Local User Accounts and Login Classes means create individual user accounts, assign appropriate login classes, avoid shared root usage, and review accounts regularly.. In practical terms, create users and assign permissions following least privilege. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Least privilege
keyIdea.text: Create individual user accounts, assign appropriate login classes, avoid shared root usage, and review accounts regularly.

content.html:
Definition › Users & Login Classes
Create a user
edit
set system login user student uid 2000 class super-user authentication plain-text-password
commit and-quit
Replace class with a restricted login class when possible; use unique UIDs for local accounts.
Best practices
  • Create individual accounts instead of sharing root.
  • Assign the minimum required privileges via login classes.
  • Consider external authentication for centralized control.
Audit
Regularly review local users and remove or disable unused entries to reduce risk.

screens.title: Commit, Rollback, and Safe Change Management
screens.subtitle: Use the transactional model to apply and safely revert configuration changes

narration.text: Junos uses a transactional configuration model: you make changes in a candidate configuration and then commit to apply them. This model allows you to prepare multiple set commands and then atomically apply them with commit, limiting partial change states. If you make an erroneous change before committing, you can use rollback 0 to discard uncommitted candidate changes and return to the last committed configuration. After a commit you can still revert by using rollback to restore a previous committed configuration; Junos keeps multiple historical commits. This is powerful for safe operations: instead of manually removing many set statements, you can roll back to a known good configuration quickly. A common mistake is attempting to run set commands from the operational prompt — those commands only work in configuration mode. Example workflow: enter configure, make your set commands, run commit and-quit to apply and exit; if an issue appears, re-enter configure and run rollback 0 or rollback 1 depending on the desired point in history. Key takeaway: adopt commit/rollback as your safety net, and make small, testable commits rather than large, risky changes.

keyIdea.title: Transactional safety
keyIdea.text: Make changes in candidate mode and use commit/rollback to apply or revert. Avoid running configuration commands in operational mode.

content.html:
Process Flow › Commit & Rollback
Typical sequence
configure
set system host-name JNCIS-Core-R1
set interfaces me0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.100.1/24
commit and-quit
If a mistake is found before commit, use rollback 0. If a committed change must be undone, use rollback <number> to restore an earlier commit.
Practical guidance
  • Make small, incremental commits that are easy to test.
  • Use rollback instead of manual reversion to avoid human error.
  • Remember set commands only work in configuration mode; an error may indicate you are still in the operational shell.

screens.title: Verification Commands and Common Troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: How to confirm your setup and fix frequent mistakes

narration.text: After performing initial configuration steps, you must verify the results using operational show commands. Two simple and powerful checks are show system host-name to confirm the hostname and show interfaces me0 terse to confirm the management interface IP and state. Use show configuration to inspect the committed configuration if you need to find an entry. If you see an error like 'set: command not recognized', the most likely cause is that you're in the operational prompt rather than configuration mode; remember to type configure or edit first. Another common troubleshooting scenario is an unreachable management interface after commit. In that case check the IP and mask, verify physical cabling, ensure the management network's gateway is reachable if configured, and confirm there is no ACL blocking the management host. Example verification commands include show system host-name, show interfaces me0 terse, and show system services. If a configuration change caused issues, use rollback 0 to restore the last commit and then reapply corrected settings. Key takeaway: verify early, use clear commands to inspect state, and know how to return to a known good configuration if needed.

keyIdea.title: Verify & troubleshoot
keyIdea.text: Use show commands to confirm hostname, interface state, and services. If commands fail, ensure you are in the correct mode and use rollback to recover.

content.html:
Check Your Understanding › Verification & Troubleshooting
Verification commands
show system host-name
show interfaces me0 terse
show configuration | display set
show system services
These commands confirm identity, interface state, full configuration in set format, and enabled services.
Troubleshooting checklist
  • If set is not recognized, switch to configuration mode with configure.
  • If me0 is unreachable, verify IP, mask, cabling, gateway, and ACLs.
  • Use rollback 0 to discard uncommitted errors or rollback <n> to restore earlier commits after a problematic commit.
Scenario
You commit a wrong IP to me0 and lose access. Reconnect via console, run rollback 0 from configuration mode to return to the last commit, correct the address, and commit again.

screens.title: Hands-on: Initial Setup Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Step through the lab activity to configure hostname, root password, me0 IP, and enable SSH

narration.text: This is a guided walkthrough for the hands-on activity described in the chapter. Assume you are connected to a factory-default Juniper device via the console. First, enter configuration mode by typing configure. Next, set the hostname with set system host-name JNCIS-Core-R1; this immediately creates a clear identity for the device and shows up in logs. Second, set the root password using set system root-authentication plain-text-password and enter a strong password when prompted. Third, configure the management interface with set interfaces me0 unit 0 family inet address 192.168.100.1/24; if your management network requires a gateway, set it appropriately. Fourth, enable SSH with set system services ssh and avoid enabling Telnet unless your lab requires it. After you have the changes ready, run commit and-quit to save and exit. Finally, verify with show system host-name and show interfaces me0 terse to confirm the hostname and that the management interface is up. If you make a mistake before commit, use rollback 0; if you need to revert a committed change, use rollback with the desired commit number. This walkthrough practices the full lifecycle: prepare, apply, verify, and recover.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: Core definitions and commands to keep in mind

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential concepts. First, the console port is your out-of-band lifeline for initial access and recovery — always have a cable and terminal ready. Second, the out-of-band management interface, typically me0 or fxp0, should be configured with an IP and placed on a secured management network, separate from the data plane. Third, protect the device by setting a strong root password immediately, then create individual user accounts with login classes to apply least privilege. Fourth, use Junos's transactional model: prepare changes in configuration mode, commit to apply, and use rollback to recover quickly if needed. Fifth, enable secure services like SSH and disable Telnet or HTTP unless absolutely required. Finally, configure system-level services — hostname, DNS, NTP, and syslog — so audits and time-based processes work reliably. Keep a habit of verifying with show commands after commit and restricting management access with ACLs or firewalls. These practices reduce downtime, improve auditability, and protect administrative access to your Juniper devices.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to use in the lab and field

narration.text: Keep three short, actionable reminders in mind during initial setup. First, always establish console access before you rely on remote tools; it's essential for recovery. Second, configure the dedicated management interface (me0 or fxp0) with a management IP, DNS, and NTP so that the device can be managed remotely and logs are accurate. Third, apply the principle of least privilege: set a strong root password, create individual local users with appropriate login classes, enable SSH for secure access, disable unused services, and use ACLs to limit management sources. These three reminders will help you keep management access both available and secure. When you return to the lab, practice the small checklist: connect console, set root password, configure me0 and SSH, commit, verify, and practice rollback. This short routine builds reliable habits for device provisioning and reduces configuration risk.
